vignette:
Mr. Pham is a small, quiet man of sixty-nine, with silver hair and fine hands that never seem to stop moving—picking at a loose thread on his sleeve, smoothing the knee of his trousers, folding and refolding a handkerchief. He speaks in a soft, careful voice, and his eyes water easily.

When he was thirty-nine, his son Minh, then five, was diagnosed with leukemia. The year that followed—the year of needles and fevers, of the smell of disinfectant and the sound of machines beeping in the dark—never left him. Minh survived. He is now a healthy thirty-five-year-old living in another city. But Mr. Pham did not survive it in the same way.

Every day now, he works as a nanny for a two-year-old boy named Leo. The job is meant to fill his days since his wife died of cancer ten years ago. He loves Leo. He is gentle, patient, tireless. But he is also afraid. Leo sneezes once in the morning, and Mr. Pham spends the rest of the day checking his temperature with a digital thermometer he carries in his pocket. He keeps a careful log—on a notepad, not on his phone, because he doesn't trust technology—of how many ounces Leo drinks, how many times he pees, the exact color of his stool. The parents tell him, kindly, that he is overdoing it. He nods in agreement and does not stop.

At night, Mr. Pham does not sleep. He lies in bed and hears the beeping of Minh's old hospital monitors, even though he has not set foot in a hospital in twenty years. He sees his wife’s face as she held Minh through the chemo, her eyes hollow and fixed. He sees the doctor's mouth moving, words he cannot remember but whose shape he still feels—a pull inside his chest, like an anchor scraping the seabed.

He does not go to the park anymore. The sight of other children running near the slide—especially children who look about five—makes his hands go cold and his heart thump so hard he thinks he might faint. He once told his daughter-in-law that he was “not a park person.” That was four months ago. Leo’s mother noticed and asked if he was okay. He said he was just tired.

He is irritable in ways he was not before. A loud noise—the clatter of a pan in the kitchen, the sudden cry of a bird outside—makes him flinch and snap at Leo, whom he never snaps at. Then he apologizes, over and over, holding the boy’s hand too tightly. He has stopped calling his son Minh. He texts him instead, short messages: *“Eat vegetables.”* *“Take vitamin.”* He cannot bear to hear his voice on the phone—it sounds too much like the little boy in the hospital bed.

His memory is strange now. He forgets where he put Leo’s sippy cup, but he remembers, in perfect detail, the pattern of the hospital curtain in room 312: little blue triangles, like a child’s drawing of mountains. He remembers the nurse’s name—Tina—and the way she hummed while changing the IV bag. He remembers the exact date Minh’s fever broke: March 14, 1995. He does not know what day it is today.

He feels, most of the time, as if he is still in that year. The years after—his wife’s illness, her funeral, the quiet apartment—all feel like a blur, like a long corridor he walked through without seeing the walls. Only the hospital room is real. Only the fear is real. And now, when Leo coughs in his sleep, Mr. Pham sits beside the crib, hand over his own mouth, trying not to shake.
